prompt: Some people believe that individual efforts to live more sustainably achieve nothing while governments fail to regulate polluting industries. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
It is often argued that personal efforts to reduce one's environmental impact are futile for as long as governments allow heavy industry to pollute freely. I largely agree that regulation is the decisive factor, but I would not accept that individual behaviour therefore counts for nothing.

The case for regulation rests on scale. The emissions produced by a single household over a lifetime are trivial beside those of one industrial plant in a year, and no amount of careful recycling closes that gap. Firms also respond to costs rather than to appeals, so an unregulated company has every incentive to push the price of its pollution onto the public. Only the state can put that cost back where it belongs, through emissions limits, carbon pricing or outright prohibition, which is why the most significant environmental gains of the past century — the removal of lead from petrol, the cleaning of industrial rivers — followed legislation rather than persuasion.

The weakness of the argument is that it treats citizens and governments as separate actors. Democratic governments legislate when the political cost of inaction rises above the cost of acting, and that calculation is shaped by what voters visibly care about. A population that has already changed its own habits is far easier to regulate than one that has not, because the policy then ratifies a shift rather than imposing one. Consumer demand also moves markets ahead of the law, as the growth in demand for electric vehicles suggests.

My view, therefore, is that individual action is not a substitute for regulation but a precondition of it. Personal restraint will not solve the problem on its own, yet it builds the constituency that makes serious legislation politically survivable, and a government that fears a backlash will not legislate at all.
title: Individual action against climate regulation
